sentences.text: Kaya's grandfather ran a wolf sanctuary in the high country of Wyoming, seven miles up a dirt road that turned into snow every October and did not turn back into road until April.
Twenty-two wolves lived there — all rescues, all animals who could not be released.
Some had been raised by people who thought they could keep a wolf as a pet.
Some had been injured in the wild and could not hunt anymore.
Some were the offspring of the ones who could not be released, born in the sanctuary and never taught to be wild.
Kaya was eleven.
She lived with her grandfather because her mother worked a long-distance job that took her overseas most of the year, and because Kaya had asked, when she was seven, to stay.
She went to school in the town at the bottom of the mountain, when the road was open.
When the road was closed, her grandfather taught her at the kitchen table.
Two winters before this story starts — when Kaya was eight and a half — a woman had brought a very small grey wolf cub to the sanctuary.
She had found it on the side of a highway, alone, and she did not know if the mother was alive.
The cub was three weeks old and would not have survived alone.

Kaya's grandfather had taken it, and Kaya had been the one who bottle-fed it, because her grandfather said young children were better than adults at raising wild things — they made less noise and moved more slowly and did not get impatient.
Kaya named the cub Ash, because she was pale grey and had a small dark stripe across her back like a smudge of soot.
Kaya raised her for four months.
She hand-fed her rabbits and small pieces of chicken as she got older.
She taught her — as much as any human can teach a wolf anything — how to be quiet in the woods.
And when Ash was seven months old, and had learned to hunt on her own, Kaya's grandfather said it was time.
"She is old enough," he said.
"She can hunt.
She has never really been tame, because we did it right.
She belongs in the woods.
If we keep her here, we make her one of ours forever.
That is not fair to her." Kaya had cried about it for a whole week before they released her.
But she had known her grandfather was right.

And so, on a cold clear morning, they drove Ash forty miles up into the mountains, and they opened the crate at the edge of a wide alpine meadow with pines at every side, and Ash stepped out slowly, and she looked back once at Kaya, and then she was gone into the trees.
Kaya had cried for two more days after that.
Her grandfather had let her.
He had said, "You loved her right, Kaya.
This is what loving her right looks like." And after those two days Kaya had felt, though it was still hard, that this was true.
And she had gone on with her life at the sanctuary.
But she had thought about Ash almost every day.
Every time she was in the woods, or when she saw a flash of grey out of the corner of her eye, she thought — Ash.
And it was never Ash.
She had made her peace with the idea that she would never see her again.
That was two winters ago.
Ash was almost three years old now — a real adult wolf, if she was still alive.
Kaya had spent both winters wondering.
Sometimes rangers reported wolf sightings in different parts of the state, and Kaya read all of them, but there was no way to know if any of them were Ash.
Her grandfather had told her, gently, that many wolves who were released did not survive their first winter.
And that this was normal.
And that even if Ash had not made it, they had done right by her.
Kaya believed this in her head.
In her heart, she still thought sometimes that Ash was out there.
She could not help it.
